articles.text: Editor: I’m writing out of great concern that the woefully under-managed Witter Field project is reaching a breaking point. It has been painfully clear since the start of this project that the District’s contractor has been leading the District around by the nose. When the Contractor says “jump” the District asks “how high?” This lack of leadership has come at great cost to the residents of Piedmont. The project’s completion date has been repeatedly pushed back through a lack of disciplined oversight, harming the District’s students, which is inexcusable. In addition, the double standard shown by the District and the City regarding parking restrictions in place for this project shows enormous disrespect to the community. Every weekday before 8:00 a.m., Palm Drive residents dutifully move their cars off of the even-numbered side of the street and scramble to find alternate parking spaces, in accordance with the agreed-upon rules for the Witter project. More times than I can count (at least a dozen), the District’s contractor has violated those same rules, with giant dump trucks rumbling down Palm Drive before the agreed start time of 8:00 a.m. These trucks often idle, engines belching noxious fumes, in front of our houses. Time and time again we have complained to the School District about these worksite violations. Time and time again we have been assured it will be addressed with the contractor. But nothing changes. The residents follow the rules, but the District does not. If a resident repeatedly violated Piedmont’s rules by having a contractor work on their house with loud power tools every day before 8:00 a.m., the City would step in with an enforcement action. In this case, the City looks away, allowing the District to break the rules. To add insult to injury to these serial violations of respect and rules, Palm Drive residents were awakened today – Saturday – by the sound of trucks grinding down Palm Drive at 7:45 a.m. to work on the Witter project. Yet again the District violated the City rules, but this time the indifference to residents was compounded because we were never informed that work would be happening on a weekend. Informing residents and taking our needs into account seems to be a very low priority for the District.

articles.text: Over a period of three years I wrote essays titled The Pandemic Diaries. Those vignettes attempted to capture in snapshot form what now already seems a distant memory. Yet for those of us who lived through those endless days and months, trailing into years, can seem surreal. I realize now I was often searching for an analog – a fragile comparison. What follows below is but one example. For millennia artists – writers, painters, sculptors, photographers, and filmmakers – have been driven to capture their meditations on periods of extreme dislocation, suffering and uncertainty. We carry with us still those images of the pandemic, of eerily empty streets and masked denizens of gowned and shielded health care workers, their exhaustion written in their vacant stares; the haunting whisper of ventilators connected to the desperately ill; stretching lines of cars waiting at food banks; school halls and classrooms eerily silent, waiting; stores, both large and small, shuttered; refrigerator trucks idling near hospitals, shrouded in a fearful finality. We lived with all of it, the arc of history bending toward the unknown. I recall coming across a photograph taken by Dorothea Lange in 1936 at the height of the Great Depression, a period in our history often used as an analog to profound social disconnection, sustained uncertainty, and economic ruination experienced by so many during the pandemic. The stark image by Lange was of a migrant mother and her three children, huddled together under a canvas lean-to tent. She is sitting, cradling a sleeping infant in her arms. A young boy stands next to her, leaning in, shielding himself, his back to the camera, as does his small sister, her face hidden behind her mother’s shoulder. articles.text: Mark 1:7 He (John the Baptist) proclaimed, “The one who is more powerful than I is coming after me; I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the thong of his sandals.” It is likely that Mark wrote his gospel primarily for the benefit of the gentile followers of Jesus living in Rome during the emperorship of Nero. Mark’s audience knew harassment, disparagement and persecution. Nero blamed them for a 64 CE fire that nearly destroyed the city. One of the messages Mark wanted to share with them was. “Jesus too knew what it was to be misunderstood and persecuted. But hold on. God is with you as God was with Jesus. The best is yet to come.” The beginning verses of Mark’s gospel are representative of the message that the best is yet to come. In them he tells of John the Baptist, whom the followers of Jesus in Rome likely had heard of, maybe even remembered, as popular, courageous, charismatic and odd, saying that though he, John, had important work to do, it was really work that was primarily to prepare the way for Jesus. John pointed beyond himself to Jesus. He was clear. The best was yet to come. The concluding verse of the passage emphasizes this theme. “I have baptized you with water; but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” John tells his audience, and through him, Mark, his hearers, that though John baptized with water, the essence of life, Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit, the essence of God. Again, the message: the best is yet to come. Children, especially as Christmas approaches, generally do not need any convincing that the best is yet to come. articles.text: On Thursday, November 30, the City of Piedmont held a public workshop regarding the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan and the city’s effort to create 132 units of new housing in the area near the Corporation Yard and Coaches Field. 60 units would be designated low-income housing. City officials said that resident input from these workshops and surveys will help City Council members prioritize features for the preferred site plan. More than 80 members of the community attended the event. City officials and consultants began the night with a presentation on the project, followed by an open house and light refreshments. Stations were set up inside the Veterans Hall, each with one of four proposed project options that differed based on their building layout. Community members were encouraged to write down their feedback for each plan on sticky notes and place them on each board. City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore and Planning Director Kevin Jackson began the event with a few words before introducing Drew Watkins, a consultant with JZMK Partners, who led the bulk of the night’s presentation. During his presentation, Watkins revealed the results of a city survey about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, detailing how coumminity members spend their time at Moraga Canyon and what improvements they would like to see. The survey received more than 1100 responses. Watkins also revealed that in all four proposed housing plans the low-income housing developments would be separate buildings from market-rate developments. When asked if the move could isolate members of low-income housing from the rest of the Piedmont community, Jackson replied that although a mixed-income housing development “would be beneficial,” financial constraints would make it difficult to find developers for it. Staff Photos Planning Director Kevin Jackson talks to community members at a workshop on November 30. Veterans Hall bustled with discussion about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan at a public meeting on Thursday, November 30. “The market doesn’t provide for developers who would do a mix of 50/50 low-income and market-rate housing in a single development. If we wanted to see housing constructed in Moraga Canyon, it was most likely that the affordable housing project would need to be separate from the market rate housing project,” said Jackson. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is part of a larger initiative by the City of Piedmont to add new housing units to the community. A mandate by the state of California requires cities to plan additional housing units in their communities to help meet housing needs across the state. The City of Piedmont was charged with creating plans to accommodate 587 units of new housing, including 257 affordable units by 2031. articles.text: I’ve been reading Michelle Obama’s new book, “The Light We Carry,” which starts out with a chapter on how knitting helped get her through the worst of the pandemic. How, in the moments when she couldn’t do anything else, she taught herself to knit, and it brought her a moment of ease and a sense of accomplishment that then helped her tackle the bigger challenges. She talks about how knitting gave her a break from her brain doing all the thinking and instead, let her hands just take over for a little while. I see this description as an absolutely perfect explanation of why creative play is so critical for all of us at all times of our lives, not just during a complete shutdown due to a worldwide pandemic. So much of our stress comes from over saturation of the stories and questions that our Knitting and other similar activities relax the mind. minds fixate on–Will my kindergartner learn how to read? How am I supposed to fight climate change when I can barely remember that I provide snacks on Tuesdays for aftercare? articles.text: Bright and early in the morning on Thanksgiving, each year the residents of Piedmont come together to be part of the annual Turkey Trot, 3.1 miles around the neighborhoods with well-wishers practically on every corner. As the participants walk, jog, or run, they are surrounded by the red and orange leaves falling from the trees, the sound of cowbells ringing in support, and crisp autumn air. Ever since I can remember, I have participated in the Turkey Trot. I remember pretending that I was asleep on the morning of the race in hopes I would be left behind and could stay in the warmth of my bed. But that never happened. I would don my shirt, racing bib, and running shoes and begrudgingly walk up Magnolia Avenue to the starting line. As the race started and people were making their way through the starting arch, I would put on my headphones and mentally prepare myself. Despite the fact that I was formerly on a cross-country team, running long distances is not my forte. But with the aid of my headphones, the trot became more bearable. I would run/walk the entire distance. Nothing beats the feeling of finally crossing the finish line and being done with the race. This year, as someone who hates running, I escaped the rigors of running by being a member of the press corps. And even though I wasn’t running, I still had to rise out of my bed at the crack of dawn to get ready. As my family and I were walking up Magnolia to the starring line, I noticed for the first time how truly quiet the streets are at that time. It wasn’t the type of quiet when everyone is asleep, but the type of quiet when there’s absolutely nobody around. As we walked closer to Highland Ave., I could hear the sound of music and someone’s voice on the microphone getting progressively louder. And soon as we walk past the high school, we see the masses of people standing at the start ready to fulfill the race motto: “Move your feet before you eat”. I took a step back, leaned against an arch at the Exedra and looked around. From my vantage point I could see all the families hyping each other up, old high school friends reuniting after being away at college, even friends from high school milling about with each other observing the race just like I was. As the race began, the announcer would call out friends that she saw. But what was important was that morale was being raised. At the start, people were smiling and in high spirits ready for the run. When the final participant crossed the start line, volunteers began to move the barriers towards the finish arch to create space for the runners when they arrived. I realized that the Turkey Trot wasn’t just a Thanksgiving race, but a real community event. In different cities and towns, I doubt that they have a similar loyal fan base, cheering on the runners at every turn of the course, and with volunteers that make the race an enjoyable experience. In Piedmont the race isn’t just an opportunity to show off one’s running skills, but an opportunity to reconnect with friends, to engage in friendly familial competition and to come together as a community to create a race that’s entertaining. As the runners started trickling to the finish line, every runner was cheered on as they came up the final hill, giving them that last bit of a boost to get across the finish line. Sometimes all you need is for one person to encourage you and your feet start moving a bit faster and you pump your arms more for that final push. Next year on Thanksgiving morning, when the sun shines and the runners get ready for the Turkey Trot, I will be with them – ready to run before the madness of last- minute meal preparations begin. Piedmont resident Larissa Edel is a junior at Bentley School.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team opened the season by winning the Bryan Ayer Classic at Lompoc High School on Saturday, December 2. In the threeday tournament, PHS dominated with a 75-5 romp over Fresno Christian on Thursday, 62-44 over Dos Pueblos of Goleta in the semifinals, and 63-37 against Orcutt Academy for the championship. Senior team captain Natalia Martinez scored 116 points in three games, including a careerhigh 43 points in Piedmont’s semifinals win over Dos Pueblos. She was named the tournament’s Most Valuable Player. Piedmont won the tournament in 2021 and did not compete in it last year. “It’s great to take these road trips; they really build the team closer together. It’s a great high school experience. Defensively, Sam Smith did a great job against some tough players; she made every shot difficult. Shalika Zuberi guarded their top shooter with pressure and toughness,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Piedmont now hosts the 2023 Paris Twins Classic from Thursday through Saturday, December 7-9. 63-37 over Orcutt Academy Piedmont led 15-7 by the end of the first quarter and jumped out to a 31-18 advantage by halftime. Piedmont limited Orcutt to just nine points in the third and put in 26 points, including 16 points from Martinez, who scored seven points from the free throw line. PHS closed out with six points in the fourth for the 63-37 win. Final stats: Martinez scored 40 points, 11 rebounds, three assists, and three steals. Sam Smith scored seven points, nine rebounds, four assist, and two steals. Lindsey Wirgler scored five points, two rebounds, five assist, and one steal. Kat Melian had four points, five rebounds. Zuberi scored seven points, two rebounds, and one steal. 62-44 over Dos Pueblos Piedmont led 15-8 by the end of the first quarter and went into halftime up 29-14 after Martinez scored 12 of Piedmont’s 14 points in the second quarter. The Highlanders pulled further ahead in the third, leading 45-26 going into the fourth with nine more points from Martinez. In the fourth, Martinez scored 13 of Piedmont’s 17 points to achieve a career high 43 points in leading PHS to a 62-44 victory. Final stats: Martinez scored 43 points, 11 rebounds, four assists. Smith scored four points, three rebounds. Wirgler had five points, two assists, and one steal. Melian had four points, eight rebounds, and one steal. Zuberi had six points, four rebounds, two steals. Photo by Todd Marshburn Shakilah Zuberi (30) is a new key player and strong defender for Piedmont.

articles.text: With renovations of Witter Field pushing back from November to February, both of Piedmont High’s soccer teams are currently displaced. The defending North Coast Section champion girls’ and boys’ teams have no home field this winter. With the season starting this week, the teams are still searching for a field for the season. “There’s a lot of organizations, schools, and clubs competing for a limited amount of field space,” said PHS Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “As we get updates on our own field it’s made things a bit difficult. There’s been multiple reasons for the completion date of Witter Field moving from November 1, when initially planned, to February, so we’ve had to adjust.” Both teams were slated to play home games at Wilder Fields in Orinda, but the City of Orinda indicated their schedules didn’t align with Piedmont’s. “I had spoken with the City of Orinda and tried to work out field availability. We thought we Staff Photos Soccer teams have been practicing at Laney College, but its field lacks lines to host soccer matches. Staff Photos With work at Witter Field scheduled through February, Piedmont High School is still searching for a site for its soccer teams. worked something out, but when we sent out our final schedules, the availability of the field had changed,” said Smet. Both PHS teams have been practicing at Laney College, but the field is unable to host games because it lacks lines for soccer. It’s an issue that isn’t easily corrected by playing all of their matches away, similar to the varsity and JV football teams this fall. Other schools are already splitting field time between boys’ and girls’ varsity, junior varsity, and freshmen soccer teams due to shortage of field space. “It’s difficult to just play all of your games away because these programs share fields. If the girls team is away, the boys might be at home, or the field might be getting used by another team,” explained veteran PHS girls’ soccer coach Dan Chubbock. With other high schools requiring field space for their own programs, turning to a nearby schools is a tough ask. Local junior colleges like Alameda and Merritt, have no lights and have other field commitments. Smet described Estuary Park in Alameda as a possible solution. The teams have played there on occasion. Chabot College, where Chubbock coaches the women’s soccer team, is another possibility. “We were in conversation with Alameda College, but it’s already in use. We have a few dates already set for Estuary Park, where we played a few times Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont is coming off two NCS titles for both boys’ and girls’ soccer teams, but face a bleak future with no home field this season.

Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team got underway by winning the 2023 Bryan Ayer Classic at Lompoc High School last weekend. We pause to take a look at three former basketball stars currently active at the collegiate level: Perseas Gioukaris of San Francisco State, Maddy Meadows of William Jessup, and Maddie Hill of Rocky Mountain University. Perseas Gioukaris San Francisco State Perseas Gioukaris, PHS Class of 2023, is a freshman at San Francisco State. She is a former starter on Piedmont’s 2023 Division 4 North Coast Section and Western Alameda County Conference championship team. San Francisco State is currently 2-4 to start its season with Gioukaris earning a role as a newcomer. So far this season, she has appeared in all six games, totaling 103 minutes with 27 points, converting 43 percent of her field goals. She’s also recorded nine rebounds, four assists, six steals, and one block. At Piedmont she earned firstteam All-League honors after being forced to miss her junior year due to CIF transfer rules. She had 12 points and two steals in Piedmont’s 75-49 win over Branson for the NCS title. Gioukaris also knocked down a critical 3-pointer in a 69-62 win over Bishop O’Dowd, Maddy Meadows William Jessup Maddy Meadows, PHS Class of 2020, is a senior at William Jessup University in Rocklin after transferring from Biola University following her sophomore year. Her team is currently 6-1 to start its season. Meadows has appeared in 84 minutes through six games, recording 31 points by converting 40 percent of her field goals, to go along with 28 rebounds, 12 assists, and four steals. In 2023, Meadows appeared in 18 games, 237 minutes and has scored 81 total points, to go along with 37 rebounds, eight assists, and 11 steals. Meadows only played her senior year at Piedmont, and helped them to a 21-7 overall record. She was named to the All-League second team. Her Rocky Mountain team is currently 7-0 to start its season. As a college freshman, Hill has appeared in four games for 29 minutes, scoring 13 points on 45 percent shooting from the field, while she’s also hit three of six 3-point attempts. At Piedmont, Maddie was a four-year starter and a key player. She earned second-team AllLeague honors as a senior. She was named by the Post Honorable Mention for Freshman of the Year in 2020.

articles.text: Photos courtesy of Rodger Sherman All of the Pac-12 mascots gather for one last photo together at the 2023 Pac-12 Championship Game, which marked the end of the storied West Coast conference. As the minutes ticked by in Saturday’s Pac-12 Championship football game between the Oregon Ducks and Washington Huskies (the Huskies won 34-31), it began to sink in. Video clips went viral of every Pac-12 mascot dancing together on the sidelines while waving goodbye to fans. It put an emphasis to the fact that December 2’s game marked the end of a 108-year-old tradition. The conference has been shattered and has left fans disillusioned. Following this weekend, California and Stanford will join the Atlantic Coastal Conference with games 3000 miles away. Heading to the Big 10 Conference are Washington, Oregon, USC, and UCLA, and joining the Big 12 Conference will be Arizona, Arizona State, Colorado, and Utah. Washington State and Oregon State, meanwhile, are still looking for a home. Something about TV revenue it seems. A lot can be made of the Pac- 12’s dissolution and finger-pointing on the cause. ad. Were USC and UCLA at fault for starting the trend in June? Can you spell G-RE-E-D? Does the blame completely rest on Pac-12 commissioner, Larry Scott, who balked at Texas joining the conference in 2010 and recently failed to get the Pac-12 Network coverage on major TV providers? What is done is done, and a new future starts. As a season ticket holder for the California Golden Bears’ football team for nearly two decades, learned about the traditions in the Pac-12 from my uncle and that is what drove my curiosity of the college game. Cal and Stanford’s Big Game, one of the best and famous rivalries in college sports, is now in an East Coast-based conference. Why would any Duke or North Carolina fan care about the Big Game, or that Cal have hoisted the Axe for three consecutive years? My fondest memories of Pac- 12 games include when DeSean Jackson had one of his legendary punt returns against Oregon in 2006 and when Marshawn Lynch hijacked a an injury cart to go joyriding on the field after defeating Washington. Jahvid Best provided some of the most electrifying moments on a football field against Oregon, UCLA, and Stanford, and lighting up this year’s Pac-12 champions, Washington, for a school-record 311 yards and four touchdowns. Many will forget that Washington was once the cupcakes of the Pac-12 conference, only for them now to spurn its historic rival in Washington State for the greener pastures of a Big 10 super conference. Time will tell what happens with the continued conference re-alignment happening in college football. But one thing is clear; the almighty dollar means school tradition plays second-fiddle to the big-business of football. – Lord Acton, English historian, politician, writer Here lies the Pac-12 Conference.

articles.text: Piedmont guitarist Jules Leyhe’s show on November 25 at the Sound Room in Oakland was a tribute to Jeff Beck performed by Jules’ band, “the Family Jules Band”. My own love of Jeff Beck goes back to 1965 when I heard the song “Heart Full Of Soul” on AM top 40 radio. I probably heard it in the car with my mom at the wheel. Beck was 21 at the time and has a very tasty guitar solo in the middle of this 2-minute,19-second song. The next song that blew my mind was also from the year 1965 – The Yardbirds doing “I’m A Man”. Both of these recordings can be heard on YouTube. The first time I heard Jeff Beck play live was at the ARMS Benefit Concert for Ronnie Lane who had multiple-sclerosis at the Cow Palace in Brisbane. The Cow Palace is where the Beatles played during their first world tour in 1964. The Rolling Stones played there the following year. The benefit concert that I saw in 1985 featured Eric Clapton doing a set followed by Jeff Beck which was followed by Jimmy Page of Led Zeppelin fame. Joe Cocker was also in the mix. I must say that Jeff Beck blew the roof off of the place with his partner Jan Hammer on keyboards. That concert can be watched on YouTube as well. Fast forward to the year 2002 to a concert Jeff Beck gave at the Warfield Theater on Market Street in San Francisco. The four of us – Mom, Dad, Sis and Bro – had been to the Great American Music Theater to hear Doc Watson on a Sunday night. Jules was about 12 years old at that time. When we were driving down Market Street with my wife at the wheel, I saw the marquee at the Warfield, which said “Jeff Beck eight and ten o’clock”. Emphatically I said, “stop the car!“ My wife, Laura, knew that I am mischievous and was about to take her 12-year-old son to a rock ‘n’ roll concert on a school night at 10 o’clock. I ran across Market Street and got two tickets in the balcony and said, “Come on Jules. We’re going to go see Jeff Beck”. And that was the night that Jules decided he was going to get serious about playing an electric guitar. He saved all his paper route and babysitting money and went down to Guitar Center to purchase a Fender Stratocaster. About one year later, I was making the bed when the phone rang. It was Jules, who said, “Dad/ Jeff Beck died!” “Oh no”, I responded. We were both crying. We were lucky to see Jeff’s third-to-last show a little over a year ago in San Jose. The next night, he played Sacramento. His last show ever was the following night in Reno. A month or two later he was gone. He died of bacterial meningitis at age 78. The Sound Room tribute show on November 25 featured Jules’ take on Jeff Beck compositions. The Family Jules Band consists of Jules Leyhe on guitar, Ian Mcardle, on keyboards, Isaac Schwartz on drums, and Matt Rhodes on bass. Ian studied at Juilliard and there is a jazz influence in his playing. Isaac is also very talented with his percussion. Isaac’s work for the Jeff Beck tribute featured both quiet, playing with brushes and mallets, as well as full tilt rock ‘n’ roll. Matt Rhodes skillfully held down the bottom with his bass guitar. The last song of the evening was a medley of the new Beatles song “Now And Then”, which Jules merged into “Beck’s Bolero” to finish the show. Everybody left The Sound Room with a smile on their face. Photo by Bob Hakins Lead guitarist Jules Leyhe and the Family Jules Band performed a tribute concert at the Sound Room on November 25 honoring the work of guitarist Jeff Beck.

articles.text: Photos by Erik Tomassan Wona Park and Wei Wang, Elizabeth Powell and Lonnie Weeks, and Nikishi Fogo in San Francisco Ballet’s Nutcracker. San Francisco Ballet announced principal casting for Nutcracker, its classic holiday production, which begins December 13. Principal Dancers Sasha De Sola, Nikisha Fogo, and Aaron Robison; as well as Soloist Jasmine Jimison and Corps de Ballet member Mingxuan Wang will dance the roles of the Sugar Plum Fairy, Grand Pas de Deux, and Queen and King of the Snow. Nutcracker is choreographed by former artistic director Helgi Tomasson, and features designs by Tony Award–winners Michael Yeargan and Martin Pakledinaz, lighting designs by James Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall Harrington. San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo leads the principal dancers and the company performed to Tchaikovsky’s iconic score. “I am both humbled and exhilarated by the boundless creativity and passion of our dancers,” said Rojo. “The enchantment of Nutcracker can already be felt throughout the city.” Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. It features the production every year with “a kaleidoscope” of more than 150 dancers. A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani. The production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks. Nutcracker is appropriate for children age five and older. No children under the age of three will be permitted. Nutcracker runs two hours with one intermission. The ballet will be shown onstage at the War Memorial Opera House through December 30. Tickets may be purchased online at www.sfballet.org or by calling Ticket Services at 415- 865-2000, open Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) opened its newest exhibition, Por el Pueblo: The Legacy and Influence of Malaquías Montoya, last month in the museum’s Great Hall. Montoyo, now 85, is originally from Albuquerque, New Mexico. He was raised by a single mother in a family of migrant farm workers in California’s Central Valley, a location that heavily inf luences his work. Montoya often uses political imagery in his work and has produced substantial art centered around the issue of immigration. His posters, graphic prints, and murals often highlighted political and social justice issues, and helped define the Chicano identity and culture for nearly 50 years. Artists from multiple generations cite Montoya as an influence, including Julio Salgado, Elyse Doyle-Martinez, Leslie Lopez, Israel Campos, and Arely Hernández. Por el Pueblo will be on view at Oakland Museum through June 30, 2024. To learn more, visit https://museumca.org/on-view/ por-el-pueblo/.

articles.text: Isaiah Stone, Jennifer Lawrence, and Ashlee Thompson in Winter’s Bone The first stark images of Winter’s Bone are of two children playing in a yard, surrounded by trees winter bare, the sunlight diffuse, without warmth. The house is more a shack than not, wood frame and hard used. Dead cars and appliances sit deep in weeds. The setting is a hamlet in the southern Missouri Ozarks, a place apart, where people – hard scrabble, insular – live on the frayed edges of society. Many exist off the grid, suspicious, even paranoid, a source of income the cooking and sale of methamphetamine. The children in the yard, a brother and sister, are the siblings of Ree Dooly (Jennifer Lawrence), 17, who carries the full weight of the family. Her mother is paralyzed by a deep depression and her father, Jessup, recently arrested for cooking meth, has just made bond and been released from jail. What Ree soon learns from the local sheriff is that in order to post bond, Jessup has put up the house and the surrounding acreage, some of it rich with timber, as collateral. If he fails to make his court date all will be forfeited. She and her family will be homeless. Ree sets out to find her father, a journey that takes her to the center of the Dolly clan where she discovers that family ties will only protect her to a certain point and no further. She’s told to leave it alone by men and women who look at her with cold eyes and grimly set mouths, their secrets impenetrable, while standing in front of houses as closed and damaged as they are. For Ree, the stakes are high, finding her father crucial, and she’s prepared to risk all. Winter’s Bone is remarkable. The performance by Lawrence is astonishing as she captures with a steely grittiness the intractable place in which Ree finds herself. As a character, Ree is the anchor of her family and alone faces a reality she barely understands. Lawrence demonstrates an uncanny subtlety and power in her portrayal, considering that the dialogue is laconic, stripped of all excess language. So authentic is this film that it borders on cinema-verite’. As the story unfolds, it’s easy to forget the actors are not locals but are delivering, like Lawrence, exceptional performances. Winter’s Bone is, at its core, a woman’s film. For all of their truculence and need to control, leavened with a subtext of violence, the men are almost peripheral. It’s the women, and, of course, Ree, who are central to the events as they slowly and ominously develop and it is the women who place Ree in harm’s way. This fact gives the story an interesting and compelling dimension. If you love movies that illuminate, that are an unsettling and penetrating window into the human condition, Winter’s Bone is not to be missed. Winter’s Bone. Directed by Debra Granik. Starring Jennifer Lawrence, John Hawkes, Dale Dickey and Garret Dillahunt. Released 2010. 1hr 39min. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/peacock/ Prime//MAX/Apple tv

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Who would’ve thought? Angelina Jolie, consummate actress, regarded as a porcelain beauty, has fashioned herself into a premier action hero, equal to any of the men doing similar genre films today. It’s been a remarkable transformation for the award-winning Jolie – Oscar for Best Supporting Actress, Golden Globe Award, Screen Actors Guild Award, all for her incomparable performance in Girl Interrupted. She also established her Indiana Jones bona fides with the Lara Croft: Tomb Raider films, followed by The Bone Collector and Gone in 60 Seconds. And not to forget Mr.& Mrs. Smith, the movie that sent the tabloids into fits of ecstasy, the icing on the celluloid cake. With the release of Salt, a let’er rip action thriller where Jolie demonstrates not only her wellhoned acting ability, but a fearless ability to leap from moving semirigs, destroy massive amounts of public property, and keep the audiences breathlessly engaged as she makes a harrowing dash from pillar to post (word is she did many of her own stunts). No matter that the plot is skinny as a swivel stick, this movie is a barn-burner with plenty of tight shots of Jolie, pursing her signature lips, contemplating her next getaway. It would be pointless to recap the convoluted plot. Sure, it’s improbably outrageous. But Salt is a flat-out gestalt of ferocious action that entertains from the first to last frame. The opening setup has her being brutally tortured by North Koreans who think she’s a spy, and the nicely done final scene which suggests its might be an introduction to a sequel. Salt. Directed by Phillip Noyce, Starring Angelina Jolie, Live Schreiber, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Andre Braugher and Daniel Olbrychski. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. articles.text: Miley Cyrus and Liam Hemsworth in The Last Song No matter what the critics may say, Nicholas Sparks is a master at what he does, though there are those who will argue that he’s a shameless manipulator of the easily accessible emotions of tweenteen girls who embrace his movies and may even read his novels. Or not. Hard to dispute that Sparks has nailed this adolescent demographic by developing a winning formula that he can superimpose on just about any love story. Recall the Dear John movie; same difference. Granted, sometimes his characters grow up, meaning they’ve grown taller. Examples would be The Notebook, Message in a Bottle and Night in Rodanthe. So, judging The Last Song from the point of view of 16-yearold girls it’s impossible to say anything other than they will love this movie and will sniffle and sigh and feel their eyes welling with tears as Sparks and director Julie Ann Robinson take them through the formulaic, rollercoaster paces. In a nutshell: Ronnie Miller (Miley Cyrus) and her brother Jonah (Bobby Coleman) are driven by their mom, Kim (Kelly Preston), to spend the summer with their dad, Steve, who lives in a spacious and chic-worn beach house on Tybee Island, off the coast of Georgia. Mom and dad are divorced. Ronnie, feeling hurt and abandoned by her dad, is perpetually angry and hostile and not happy to be spending a weekend let alone a summer on the island. These are emotions that she shares at every opportunity. She pouts and snarls and stalks off in all directions. Until she meets Will (Liam Hensworth), an island resident, beach volleyball player, summer mechanic, who, like Ronnie, has just graduated from high school and is waiting to go to Vanderbilt University in the fall. Ronnie, a piano prodigy, has been accepted to Julliard for a full ride but refuses to go and, for good measure, refuses to play. She’s too angry and believes she will hurt her father, a composer, by walking away from her scholarship and her talent. Sparks is a master of girl meets boy girl on the beach, followed by boy pursues girl hoping to ignite a nascent spark. In this case, Ronnie practices complete indifference to Will’s attention (you can almost hear that quintessentially terrible teen word, “whatever,” trailing Ronnie from house to beach and back), while keeping her nose buried in Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina. When Ronnie discovers endangered sea turtle eggs in front of the beach house, she sets about trying to protect them from raccoons. Will, volunteering for a marine sanctuary, shows up to stand vigil with her. Romance takes hold and angry, indifferent Ronnie gets less angry and way less indifferent with everyone, her dad included. And so Sparks sets the hook, and, just to be sure, includes engaging montages of Will and Ronnie swimming, playing tag, getting in a mud fight, talking intensely, meeting his parents (he’s hugely wealthy) and, indeed, kissing. Lots of kissing. All chaste and lovely and very emotive. Of course, Sparks loves to pump up the volume regarding unfinished issues, pre-fab subplots and misunderstandings, willing to throw in, predictably, a terminal illness or an unsettling speed bump just to keep things interesting. And just when you thought it was safe to put away the tissue. Now remember who’s sitting in the audience, all those teen girls identifying with Ronnie and loving every moment. By that measure, The Last Song succeeds and then some, making Nicholas Sparks happy and rich and very good at what he does: gently and not so gently squeezing the hearts of tween-teen girls who love every minute. One last thing: The Last Song is a transition film for Miley who has paid her dues as Hannah Montana, a long-running tween-teen television show of the same name, one that became a cultural event for young girls. She’s been a phenom who has grown up on television. She can sing. But can she act and so carry a feature film? Perhaps a better question is: Is she credible to young people in the role of a girl with issues who finds herself on the cusp of becoming a woman? Answer: indeed. The Last Song. Directed by Julie Ann Robinson. Starring Miley Cyrus, Liam Hensworth, Greg Kinnear, Bobby Coleman and Kelly Preston. Released in 2010. Rated PG. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+/Apple tv.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Star Wars: The Force Awakens is the seventh in what is one of the most successful franchises in film history. Over the decades, starting in May 1977, the generic Star Wars has morphed into a cultural phenom, one that has captured the imaginations of moviegoers globally. They remain popular even when the sequels and prequels didn’t quite reach the bar established with the initial trilogy, Star Wars IV: A New Hope, The Empire Strikes Back, and Return of the Jedi. Woven through all the Star Wars films is the question: what is there about these stories, these characters, that is so compelling and has consistently resonated with wide-ranging audiences? Perhaps the genius of George Lucas was in crafting a blend of high tech/low tech medieval lore (Princesses, Jedi Knights, mystical swords and dark Lords), combined with storytelling similar to mid-20th century Republic serials that kids flocked to movie theaters every Saturday to watch cliff-hanging installments of action movies like Don Winslow of the Navy and Flash Gordon. And hands down, there’s never been a better example of a character from the dark side than Darth Vader (aka Lord Vader), surrounded by armed storm troopers, his menacing black mask covering a visage we can only imagine, every breath a wheezing sound. His persona – voice and stature – was inspired and breathtaking. This was sci-fi fantasy unlike anything we had seen before. And so began a narrative that would span three movies and would introduce a galaxy far, far away that was both myth and entertainment, proving to be irresistible. Ultimately, these films, and now The Force Awakens. are wonderfully constructed morality plays, primal fantasies that reduce our complex world to good vs. evil. The loosely structured band of Rebels – never ominously militaristic – also represents the best impulses of men and women who yearn for Democracy. And they still possess those familiar X-Wing fighters, while remaining ready to confront Fascism’s jackbooted soldiers and their deadly armaments, to include a Death Star equipped with a planet-destroying ray. The Force Awakens is the first installment of a fresh trilogy that introduces a new generation of characters such as Rey (Daisy Ridley), a space junk scavenger; and Finn (John Boyega), a reluctant storm trooper; as well as Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac), a hotshot Resistance pilot sent in search of Luke Skywalker. And not to forget Darth Vader’s masked acolyte, Kylo Ren (Adam Driver), who kneels at the feet of the supreme leader, Snoke (Andy Serkis), one very large dude. The story manages to skirt a precipice of nostalgia while avoiding being maudlin as it builds a bridge between the original trilogy, featuring Han Solo (Harrison Ford), Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher) who is now a general in the Resistance, and Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill). Clearly, the coming films will focus on what will be the ongoing battle in all its permutations between The Resistance and The Front. So, if The Force Awakens is considered in great part prologue, then some of the best is yet to come. In essence it is the first reboot of the initial Star Wars and pays homage to those first three films that so completely solidified the brand. For those proto-fans who sat down for the first time back in 1977 and watched the yellow block script scroll slowly into the dark distance, words that framed the battles ahead, even today that moment remains unforgettable. But that was then and this is now. Kids having the same experience with The Force Awakens won’t be disappointed. The force is beginning to awaken. Wait for it. Star Wars: The Force Awakens. The Last Song tests emotions of teen girls Miley Cyrus and Liam Hemsworth in The Last Song By Chris Honoré No matter what the critics may say, Nicholas Sparks is a master at what he does, though there are those who will argue that he’s a shameless manipulator of the easily accessible emotions of tweenteen girls who embrace his movies and may even read his novels. Or not. Hard to dispute that Sparks has nailed this adolescent demographic by developing a winning formula that he can superimpose on just about any love story. Recall the Dear John movie; same difference. Granted, sometimes his characters grow up, meaning they’ve grown taller. Examples would be The Notebook, Message in a Bottle and Night in Rodanthe. So, judging The Last Song from the point of view of 16-yearold girls it’s impossible to say anything other than they will love this movie and will sniffle and sigh and feel their eyes welling with tears as Sparks and director Julie Ann Robinson take them through the formulaic, rollercoaster paces. In a nutshell: Ronnie Miller (Miley Cyrus) and her brother Jonah (Bobby Coleman) are driven by their mom, Kim (Kelly Preston), to spend the summer with their dad, Steve, who lives in a spacious and chic-worn beach house on Tybee Island, off the coast of Georgia. Mom and dad are divorced. Ronnie, feeling hurt and abandoned by her dad, is perpetually angry and hostile and not happy to be spending a weekend let alone a summer on the island. These are emotions that she shares at every opportunity. She pouts and snarls and stalks off in all directions. Until she meets Will (Liam Hensworth), an island resident, beach volleyball player, summer mechanic, who, like Ronnie, has just graduated from high school and is waiting to go to Vanderbilt University in the fall. Ronnie, a piano prodigy, has been accepted to Julliard for a full ride but refuses to go and, for good measure, refuses to play. She’s too angry and believes she will hurt her father, a composer, by walking away from her scholarship and her talent. Sparks is a master of girl meets boy girl on the beach, followed by boy pursues girl hoping to ignite a nascent spark. In this case, Ronnie practices complete indifference to Will’s attention (you can almost hear that quintessentially terrible teen word, “whatever,” trailing Ronnie from house to beach and back), while keeping her nose buried in Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina. When Ronnie discovers endangered sea turtle eggs in front of the beach house, she sets about trying to protect them from raccoons. Will, volunteering for a marine sanctuary, shows up to stand vigil with her. Romance takes hold and angry, indifferent Ronnie gets less angry and way less indifferent with everyone, her dad included. And so Sparks sets the hook, and, just to be sure, includes engaging montages of Will and Ronnie swimming, playing tag, getting in a mud fight, talking intensely, meeting his parents (he’s hugely wealthy) and, indeed, kissing. Lots of kissing. All chaste and lovely and very emotive. Of course, Sparks loves to pump up the volume regarding unfinished issues, pre-fab subplots and misunderstandings, willing to throw in, predictably, a terminal illness or an unsettling speed bump just to keep things interesting. And just when you thought it was safe to put away the tissue. Now remember who’s sitting in the audience, all those teen girls identifying with Ronnie and loving every moment. By that measure, The Last Song succeeds and then some, making Nicholas Sparks happy and rich and very good at what he does: gently and not so gently squeezing the hearts of tween-teen girls who love every minute. One last thing: The Last Song is a transition film for Miley who has paid her dues as Hannah Montana, a long-running tween-teen television show of the same name, one that became a cultural event for young girls. She’s been a phenom who has grown up on television. She can sing. But can she act and so carry a feature film? Perhaps a better question is: Is she credible to young people in the role of a girl with issues who finds herself on the cusp of becoming a woman? Answer: indeed. The Last Song. It was recalled that in the early 20th century Piedmont real estate and transportation development were closely linked. People needed to be able to get from their homes to work. Paths and stairs to Key System streetcars were often the solution. The walkers had heard of the Key System’s Transbay C Line that ran through Piedmont to Oakland and San Francisco in the first half of the century. There was also the Trestle Glen B Line. The Trestle Glen neighborhood was developed around the B Line in the early 1900s. Access to the trains was possible via paths from Trestle Glen Road, Underhills Road (which runs parallel to Trestle Glen), and other nearby streets. The B-line went down 22nd Street (now Grand Avenue) past Lake Merritt, turned on Lake Park Avenue, passed the Grand Lake Theater, and then turned up Lakeshore Avenue onto a private right-ofway, now the location of Bank of the West. The B Line train began service to San Francisco from the Underhills station on April 20, 1958. Just like Piedmont after the rails were removed, new homes were built on portions of the right of way. Some homeowners extended their back yards on to the former B-train route. Off they went down Highland Avenue. up Sheridan, Wildwood, Crocker, and Hampton to the top of St. James Drive, continuing to St. James Place, where they took a group photo. The stairs were steep and the walkers were glad there was a hand rail. There was only a low concrete railing beside the 151-foot set of stairs, but the walkers took their time and climbed back to St. James Drive. The group retraced their steps back to town center with appreciation for Mike identifying a great walk for them. On the way back the skies fully cleared and it was a beautiful morning, just as it always is for the Wednesday walkers. articles.text: Anne Elizabeth Hendrick Gaston MD died peacefully on November 24, 2023, in Atlanta, Georgia. She was a loving wife of sixty-seven years, and an honorable, dedicated, and talented, physician, who was beloved by her many patients, family, and friends. She was a most caring mother, grandmother, and a new great-grandmother. Dr. Gaston was 93 years old. Born Anne Elizabeth Hendrick on November 10, 1930, in Columbus, Georgia, she attended her local schools in Hurtsboro, Alabama in a class of 12 students. She received her undergraduate degree from the University of Alabama in only three years in 1951, and then her medical degree at Emory University in 1955 as one of only two women in her class. At Emory she met and married classmate Harper Gaston, who also became a doctor. She was a Board Certified Neonatologist and Board Certified Pediatrician. In 1961, Drs. Anne and Harper Gaston moved from Atlanta to Piedmont, California, where they joined the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group in the KPMG’s first medical office in San Leandro, California. Their decision to move to California was based primarily upon the fact that the KPMG was one of the only medical groups in the country which would allow both a husband and wife to work at the same time, and to be paid equally for their work. Dr. Anne Gaston worked for the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group of Northern California for over twenty years, and she recently became the oldest female physician of the Northern California Kaiser Permanente Medical Group. Dr Anne Gaston took the first US Neonatology Board exams and as a newly certified Neonatologist, helped to establish all surprises and entertaining her friends, and loved her ever-cultivated collection of orchids, and traveling throughout the world as a tourist and physician. In Atlanta, Dr. Gaston continued her community service, by serving on the Board of Trustees of Emory University (1990- 1996) and the Emory Alumni Association Board of Governors where she was a founding member (1988-1993) and served on the Medical School Alumni Board (2001-2010), She was an emerita member and in many other capacities for over 50 years, including serving as the first woman elected as a School of Medicine Class President. Dr. Gaston was awarded the Emory Medal in 1996, Emory’s highest honor, for her service to Emory and the community. The Drs. Gaston also established the Gaston Service Scholarships for Emory University Medical School students who exemplify community volunteerism and service. “Service in and of itself is the greatest reward that our profession can offer us. It is the heart of medicine,” she once said. A private service was held on Saturday, December 2, 2023, where she will be laid to rest in her hometown in the Hurtsboro, Alabama Methodist Church Cemetery. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Oatmeal persimmon cookies are a great winter treat with abundance of persimmons in town. Four generations in my family look forward to these cookies when persimmons are at their peak season. That’s now, and it conveniently coincides with cookie season. The recipe is from the late- 70’s or early-80’s judging from a handwritten recipe card I pulled from my mom’s recipe collection. I’d given it to her years ago, and this season she’s already baked three batches to share with family, including my grandchildren. If you’re fortunate, you have a persimmon tree or neighbors who’ll share their bumper crop. Otherwise, persimmons are plentiful at markets this time of year, too. This recipe uses the Hachiya variety (with a pointy tip), which ripens to a soft, squishy jam-like consistency. When you scoop out the pulp for this recipe, it will be like a mashed, ripe banana. These are soft, chewy cookies with a nice texture from the oats, nuts, and fruit. I added dried cranberries as a nod to the holidays, but we typically do not include them. They may not be the fanciest looking cookies, but they will be among the most flavorful. Oatmeal Persimmon Cookies Makes about 60 2” cookies INGREDIENTS • 3/4 cup unsalted butter, room temperature soft • 3/4 cup brown sugar • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 1 cup persimmon pulp from squishy-ripe Hachiya variety • 1 teaspoon baking soda • 2 eggs, extra-large, room temperature • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1-1/2 cup all-purpose flour • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1 teaspoon cinnamon, ground • 1/2 teaspoon nutmeg, ground

pages.text: Wednesday, December 6, 2023 25 Oatmeal Persimmon cookies…Mmmm good Photo by Deborah Quok Oatmeal persimmon cookies are a great winter treat with abundance of persimmons in town. By Deborah Quok Four generations in my family look forward to these cookies when persimmons are at their peak season. That’s now, and it conveniently coincides with cookie season. The recipe is from the late- 70’s or early-80’s judging from a handwritten recipe card I pulled from my mom’s recipe collection. I’d given it to her years ago, and this season she’s already baked three batches to share with family, including my grandchildren. If you’re fortunate, you have a persimmon tree or neighbors who’ll share their bumper crop. Otherwise, persimmons are plentiful at markets this time of year, too. This recipe uses the Hachiya variety (with a pointy tip), which ripens to a soft, squishy jam-like consistency. When you scoop out the pulp for this recipe, it will be like a mashed, ripe banana. These are soft, chewy cookies with a nice texture from the oats, nuts, and fruit. I added dried cranberries as a nod to the holidays, but we typically do not include them. They may not be the fanciest looking cookies, but they will be among the most flavorful. Oatmeal Persimmon Cookies Makes about 60 2” cookies INGREDIENTS • 3/4 cup unsalted butter, room temperature soft • 3/4 cup brown sugar • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 1 cup persimmon pulp from squishy-ripe Hachiya variety • 1 teaspoon baking soda • 2 eggs, extra-large, room temperature • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1-1/2 cup all-purpose flour • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1 teaspoon cinnamon, ground • 1/2 teaspoon nutmeg, ground • • • • • • 1/2 teaspoon cloves, ground 1/2 teaspoon sea salt 1-1/2 cup rolled oats 1 cup walnuts, coarsely chopped 3/4 cup dried cranberries, preferably unsweetened 1/2 cup coconut flakes, unsweetened INSTRUCTIONS Sift together the all-purpose flour, baking powder, ground spices and salt into a medium bowl. Set aside. In a large mixing bowl, cream together the butter and sugars until light and fluffy. Beat in the eggs until combined. Add the vanilla extract. In a small bowl, stir the baking soda into the persimmon pulp, then add to the creamed mixture. The mixture may curdle but it will be fine when the dry ingredients are added. Add the sifted dry ingredients. Mix just until combined. Fold in the rolled oats, chopped walnuts, dried cranberries (if using), and coconut flakes. Refrigerate the cookie dough at least six hours, up to overnight. This allows the flour and oats to absorb moisture and firms the dough for easy handling. When ready to bake, position oven racks to divide the oven in thirds. Preheat the oven to either 325° F on the convection-bake setting or 350° F regular bake setting. Line cookie sheet pans with parchment paper. Scoop the cookie dough by scant, rounded tablespoonfuls onto the parchment-lined baking sheets spaced at least 1-inch apart. Bake for about 12 minutes, rotating the pans as needed for even baking, until browned and cookie tops spring back to a light touch. Let rest on the baking sheet for a minute or two to firm up, then transfer to a wire rack to cool completely. Store in an airtight container. A sheet of parchment paper between any layered cookies helps prevent sticking. articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on December 9, 2020. Paris, the City of Lights, is magical at Christmas, but while different, this year has many similar traditions. The lights turned up last week inside department stores and neighborhood shops. The store openings were widely heralded after Parisians endured the entire month of November on lockdown. Retailers were chomping at the bit for Christmastime shopping to begin as they try to climb out of the disastrous sales in 2020. Street trees and store windows are dressed up in their best holiday goldware, twinkling seductively for shoppers to hurry in. The temperature is chilly with misty showers and sidewalks full of people and shopping bags, so it feels just like a normal Christmas. Starting December 4th Black Friday sales were everywhere, with featured goods up to 50% off as a way to bring in the hordes. We’re not sure people know what Black Friday is, but the concept, not unlike the United States, starts after Thanksgiving when merchants start to hope that the winding-down selling days for the year begin to move from red ink deficient to black ink and create prosperity. A Parisian symbol of the City of Lights and an oasis for shopping is Galleries Lafayette, which occupies the entire block of Boulevard Haussmann on the Right Bank. After a metro ride, we exited at Rue de la Chaussée D’Antin, where we climbed out of the cavernous underground to the reveal of flashing, vividly hued window displays. Galleries was a luxury bazaar by design, and this is the 1912 Flagship store. It’s on everybody’s must-see list for its spectacular steel and glass dome, a department store inspired for the theater world and Paris Opera. The founders pioneered production of store-brand merchandise: high-fashion styles that were well-made and sold at budget prices. Still very much their marketing edge, this successful enterprise has expanded to 62 Galleries Lafayette locations worldwide. Each Christmas the largest tree imaginable is suspended from the dome. The holiday-decked main floor is wall-to-wall boutiques for cosmetics, perfumes, and accessories, amid hanging displays of color-rich cheer covering every wall and ceiling – or so it seems. It’s a good browse riding the escalators from floor to floor and strolling through beautifully designed displays in its departments. At the main store’s third floor, a glass footbridge allows visitors to cross Rue de la Chaussée D’Antin to Galleries pour Hommes. Across Boulevard Haussmann is Galleries Epicure. We left the Galleries before fulfilling our shoppers’ duty to buy and resisted the pastry kiosk craftily placed at the exit door. We will ourselves to leave and go home for dinner. Christmas Markets The much-loved Christmas Markets have arrived, and although several (Notre Dame Cathedral, Swedish, Alsace at Gare de L’Est) canceled their season due to Covid-19, the markets are spread throughout the Paris districts and located in Saint-Germain des Prés, Les Halles, Place Vendôme (The Ritz), and Hôtel de Ville. Many market shoppers are delighted with the rows of traditional wooden chalet booths with a variety of items for sale: ornaments, handmade craft items, arts and unique objects, holiday foods and produce; ideas for gifts, greenery, and so on. The Christmas Markets originating in Alsace and Germany have more recently been popularized as essential to the holiday season. https://www.parisdiscoveryguide. com/paris-events-december.html Concerts and other venues Standing concerts are scheduled tentatively for the Christmas season, but the exact regulations for capacity are yet being worked out. The same is true for clubs and nightclubs, which don’t yet have a resumption date. Movie theaters, museums, and theaters may be open again starting December 15; however the seating capacity is yet to be announced. Further, the curfew in Paris will remain from 9 p.m. to 7 a.m., which presents questions about event attendees out past curfew and the necessary retention of ticket stubs to avoid a curfew violation with a penalty of €135. That ticket is plenty lofty to ruin an otherwise pleasant evening out for a movie. Here’s a guide to the Paris Church concerts for the holiday season: https://www.parisdiscoveryguide.com/paris-church-concerts.html Shoppers wait to cross at a stoplight outside Galleries Lafayette main store. French News Restaurants and bars will be permitted to reopen in France but not until January 20. It’s been a long slog stuck on idle when typically the City hosts the biggest parties of the season. The Covid- 19 consequences are heartbreaking and breaking the bank of many businesses. As many as 30% of Paris bars and restaurants are expected to close for good. Covid-19 has infected 68 million people worldwide and the tally of deaths is approaching 1.6 million. Mask-wearing continues to be compulsory in France, and people are asked to maintain social distancing. France and U.S. share commonality in the Covid-19 epidemic, which is still not under control. France, too, has rebel merchants and individuals taking a stand against lockdown; but the French do not arm themselves or refuse to wear masks. Covid cases and deaths are rising at a fearful rate, and ICU beds in hospitals are nearing capacity. The images from the Depression are vastly different from ours today, yet in many ways they are the same. Our neighborhoods were silent, doors closed, drapes tightly drawn, families, friends, perhaps strangers waiting inside. Unspeaking masked shoppers walking apart, stood in hushed lines in grocery stores and pharmacies, waiting to pay, taking creased bills in change, wondering whose hands they had passed through.
